 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(t)

  f.write(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n'+p.extract_text())
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()[:52000])
PY"

strengths: R2E offers a coherent contribution to biomedical NLP: candidate-specific retrieval, masked entity representations, and evidence-level Shapley attribution make individual prediction scores inspectable. Training with missing evidence supports the attribution procedure.

The results support useful predictive performance without sacrificing access to evidence. On Gene Description Facts, uncorrected R2E improves MRR from the MLM baseline’s 0.167 to 0.202; literature-only clinical AUROC is comparable to MLM (0.632 versus 0.630), consistent with the paper’s stated aim.

Training from scratch, document-level corpus splits, and temporal restrictions on literature are thoughtful controls. Component ablations and experiments incorporating newer evidence without retraining provide additional support for the architecture.

The three released evaluation benchmarks are valuable resources. The appendices document architecture, hyperparameters, prompts, dataset construction, attribution algorithms, and computational costs extensively.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains a substantial concern. The training corpus includes licensed material, entity linking relies on proprietary dictionaries and models, and the paper explicitly withholds training data, code, and weights. Detailed architectural documentation and evaluation datasets enable partial reimplementation but leave no demonstrated route to reproducing the reported system. An accessible checkpoint or a reproducible public-corpus experiment would materially strengthen the case for Findings.

The explanation evaluation establishes less than the broader scientific-reasoning claims suggest. Shapley values attribute scores relative to the chosen NULL baseline; this does not establish biological validity. Clinical evidence relevance AUROC against GPT-4 is only 0.665. Human validation covers eight hypotheses per task, with clinical examples selected by expert familiarity, and reports GPT-4–human agreement rather than direct Shapley–human alignment. Direct expert evaluation and attribution stability measurements would strengthen this central contribution.

The temporal controls do not cover all reported clinical variants. Genetics evidence comes from a 2024 resource without a documented historical availability cutoff, and GPT-4 auditing introduces knowledge not restricted to pre-2005. Consequently, combined-evidence and audited results do not establish prediction using only information available before the trials. The literature-only results remain informative, but the prospective interpretation needs qualification.

Clinical outcomes are imperfect proxies for the claimed confirmation of efficacy. Appendix P treats discontinued Phase II/III development as failure and pre-registration or later stages as success. These labels conflate efficacy with commercial, pharmacological, and development decisions; pre-registration also does not establish regulatory approval. The acknowledged label noise warrants narrower claims and validation against explicitly documented efficacy outcomes.

The frequency-correction analysis needs both a mathematical clarification and a fairer comparison. Section 3.4 excludes the positive entity when sampling negatives, whereas Appendix F assumes independent uniform sampling. Under the stated procedure, the negative conditional is (1-p(a|q))/(|A|-1), so Equation 9 is not exact. Additionally, the main ranking comparisons omit a frequency-corrected MLM despite deriving that correction in Appendix G, leaving the contribution of retrieval versus prior adjustment insufficiently isolated.
